sources.ref_file_title: BM88 - Arthur-merlin games A randomized proof system and a hierarchy of complexity classes
sources.note: Journal version of Babai's STOC 1985 paper 'Trading group theory for randomness' (pp. 421-429), which introduced the MA/AM hierarchy and proved MA ⊆ AM; BM88 is the wiki's existing page and the standard citation.

pages.class_justification: Unconditional containment between complexity classes; by repo convention (cf. bpp-to-am-gs86, qcma-to-qma) such inclusions carry class free.
pages.statement: $\classMA \subseteq \classAM$: every language with a [[merlin-arthur|Merlin–Arthur]] proof system has an [[arthur-merlin|Arthur–Merlin]] proof system — [[BM88 - Arthur-merlin games A randomized proof system and a hierarchy of complexity classes|BM88]].
pages.sketch: Amplify the MA verifier's soundness error below $2^{-\ell}/3$ by parallel repetition, where $\ell$ bounds the length of Merlin's message, then swap the order: Arthur sends his coins first and Merlin answers. A union bound over the $2^{\ell}$ possible Merlin messages bounds the soundness error of the swapped protocol by $1/3$; completeness is unaffected.
flags: The migrated parenthetical ('Merlin's optimal strategy is independent of those coins') is not a proof; the statement and sketch replace it with the amplify-then-swap argument.
Frontmatter source: folklore should become the BM88 citation; MA ⊆ AM is a theorem (Babai 1985 / Babai–Moran 1988), not folklore.
verifier_changes: sketch: amplification target 2^{-(ℓ+1)} → 2^{-ℓ}/3 so the swapped protocol meets the 1/3 soundness bound; noted completeness is unaffected

sources.ref_file_title: Ver92 - On the Power of PP
sources.note: Proc. 7th Annual Structure in Complexity Theory Conference, IEEE, 1992, pp. 138-143. Proves MA ⊆ PP and gives an oracle relative to which AM ⊄ PP. Not in cryptobib; needs inline bibtex.

pages.class_justification: Unconditional containment between complexity classes; repo convention assigns class free to such inclusions.
pages.statement: $\classMA \subseteq \classPP$: every language with a [[merlin-arthur|Merlin–Arthur]] proof system is decidable in unbounded-error [[probabilistic-polynomial-time|probabilistic polynomial time]] — [[Ver92 - On the Power of PP|Ver92]].
pages.sketch: Amplify the MA verifier's error below $2^{-(\ell+2)}$, where $\ell$ bounds the witness length. The PP machine samples a uniform witness and runs the amplified verifier: for $x \in L$ it accepts with probability at least $2^{-\ell}(1 - 2^{-(\ell+2)}) \ge \tfrac{3}{4} \cdot 2^{-\ell}$, for $x \notin L$ with probability at most $2^{-(\ell+2)}$; the threshold $2^{-(\ell+1)}$ separates the two cases, and shifting a PP threshold is standard.

sources.ref_file_title: BN00 - Authenticated Encryption Relations among Notions and Analysis of the Generic Composition Paradigm
sources.note: cryptobib_key: AC:BelNam00 (verified in vendor/cryptobib/crypto.bib, LNCS 1976, pp. 531-545; eprint 2000/025). Journal version: J. Cryptology 21(4), 2008 (JC:BelNam08). Proves encrypt-then-MAC with a strongly unforgeable MAC is INT-CTXT, that IND-CPA + INT-CTXT implies IND-CCA, and that a weakly unforgeable MAC does not suffice.

sources.ref_file_title: KY00 - Unforgeable Encryption and Chosen Ciphertext Secure Modes of Operation
sources.note: cryptobib_key: FSE:KatYun00 (verified in vendor/cryptobib/crypto.bib, LNCS 1978, pp. 284-299; the proceedings volume is dated 2001). Independent concurrent work: ciphertext unforgeability plus IND-CPA implies IND-CCA for symmetric encryption.

pages.class_justification: Encrypt-then-MAC is one fixed construction invoking the SKE scheme's $\Enc$/$\Dec$ and the MAC's $\Tag$/$\Vrfy$ only as oracles; the security reduction runs any CCA adversary as an oracle, answering decryption queries by rejecting every ciphertext-tag pair not produced by the encryption oracle and outputting an accepted fresh pair as a MAC forgery. This is the RTV04 fully-black-box shape.
pages.statement: Let $\SKE$ be a [[symmetric-key-encryption#cpa-security|CPA-secure]] [[symmetric-key-encryption|SKE]] scheme and $\MAC$ a strongly unforgeable (SUF-CMA) [[message-authentication-code|MAC]]. Encrypt-then-MAC — encrypt under an SKE key, then tag the ciphertext under an independent MAC key — is a [[symmetric-key-encryption#cca-security|CCA-secure]] SKE scheme. Weak unforgeability does not suffice: with a merely UF-CMA MAC the composition can fail CCA security — [[BN00 - Authenticated Encryption Relations among Notions and Analysis of the Generic Composition Paradigm|BN00]].
pages.sketch: Decryption returns $\bot$ unless $\Vrfy(k_m, c, t) = 1$. Strong unforgeability of $\MAC$ ensures every decryption query $(c, t)$ not returned by the encryption oracle is rejected except with negligible probability, so the reduction to CPA security of $\SKE$ answers all fresh decryption queries with $\bot$.
pages.improvements_text: - Independently and concurrently: ciphertext unforgeability plus CPA security implies CCA security for symmetric encryption — [[KY00 - Unforgeable Encryption and Chosen Ciphertext Secure Modes of Operation|KY00]].
flags: Hypothesis 'ske' must be read as CPA-secure SKE and 'mac' as SUF-CMA; the wiki's MAC page defines only (weak) UF-CMA, so the SUF-CMA qualifier lives in prose. A strong-unforgeability section on message-authentication-code.md would make it linkable.

pages.wrong_reason: False as stated under the standard simulation-based definitions: security against malicious adversaries does not imply security against (plain) semi-honest adversaries. The malicious-model simulator may substitute the corrupted party's input in the ideal execution, while the semi-honest simulator must reproduce the party's view on its actual input; there are protocols secure against malicious adversaries that are not secure against semi-honest ones. Documented in Hazay–Lindell, 'A Note on the Relation between the Definitions of Security for Semi-Honest and Malicious Adversaries' (eprint 2010/551, existence and content verified via search snippets) and in Goldreich's Foundations of Cryptography Vol. 2 (augmented semi-honest model, §7.4.4.1). The correct nearby edge is: malicious security implies AUGMENTED semi-honest security (semi-honest adversaries additionally allowed to substitute their input before the execution starts).
flags: If the corrected edge (malicious => augmented semi-honest) is wanted, source it to Goldreich Foundations Vol. 2 §7.4.4 and/or Hazay–Lindell eprint 2010/551, and add an augmented-semi-honest variant anchor first.

sources.authors: Léo Ducas, Eike Kiltz, Tancrède Lepoint, Vadim Lyubashevsky, Peter Schwabe, Gregor Seiler, Damien Stehlé

sources.authors: Eike Kiltz, Vadim Lyubashevsky, Christian Schaffner

sources.ref_file_title: BBD+23 - Fixing and Mechanizing the Security Proof of Fiat-Shamir with Aborts and Dilithium
sources.authors: Manuel Barbosa, Gilles Barthe, Christian Doczkal, Jelle Don, Serge Fehr, Benjamin Grégoire, Yu-Hsuan Huang, Andreas Hülsing, Yi Lee, Xiaodi Wu
sources.note: cryptobib_key: C:BBDDFG23 (verified in vendor/cryptobib/crypto.bib, pp. 358-389). eprint 2023/246.

pages.class_justification: No source states an RTV-style class; the ROM proof rewinds the adversary via the forking lemma and is scoped to an idealized model, so recording a class would add a claim the sources do not make.
pages.model_justification: DKL+18 prove unforgeability in the (classical and quantum) random-oracle model: the challenge hash of Fiat–Shamir with aborts is modeled as a random oracle. Frontmatter currently says standard and must change to rom.
pages.statement: Dilithium, the basis of ML-DSA (FIPS 204), is a Fiat–Shamir-with-aborts [[digital-signature|signature]] scheme over module lattices. In the random-oracle model it is [[digital-signature#strong-unforgeability|SUF-CMA]] (hence EUF-CMA) secure assuming hardness of [[learning-with-errors#module-lwe|Module LWE]] and [[shortest-integer-solution#module-sis|Module-SIS]]; the reduction from Module-SIS goes through the forking lemma and is non-tight — [[DKL+18 - CRYSTALS-Dilithium A Lattice-Based Digital Signature Scheme|DKL+18]].
pages.sketch: The signer samples a short masking vector $\mathbf{y}$, commits to the high bits of $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{y}$, derives the challenge $c$ by hashing the commitment with the message, and releases $\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{y} + c\mathbf{s}_1$ only if rejection sampling passes, so signatures are independent of the secret. Module LWE makes the public key $(\mathbf{A}, \mathbf{t} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{s}_1 + \mathbf{s}_2)$ pseudorandom, and forking a forger on the challenge yields a short nonzero vector in the kernel of $[\mathbf{A} \mid \mathbf{t} \mid \mathbf{I}]$, a Module-SIS solution.
pages.security_loss: Non-tight in the classical ROM: the reduction from Module-SIS goes through the forking lemma. The QROM bound is tight only under the additional SelfTargetMSIS assumption (KLS18).
pages.improvements_text:
- QROM security: Dilithium-QROM, a larger-parameter variant with a lossy identification scheme, is tightly secure in the QROM under Module LWE; the original Dilithium is QROM-secure under Module LWE, Module-SIS and the new SelfTargetMSIS assumption — [[KLS18 - A Concrete Treatment of Fiat-Shamir Signatures in the Quantum Random-Oracle Model|KLS18]].
- A gap in the Fiat–Shamir-with-aborts security proofs, including Dilithium's, is identified and repaired with machine-checked proofs in the ROM and QROM — [[BBD+23 - Fixing and Mechanizing the Security Proof of Fiat-Shamir with Aborts and Dilithium|BBD+23]].

sources.ref_file_title: BDK+18 - CRYSTALS-Kyber A CCA-Secure Module-Lattice-Based KEM
sources.authors: Joppe W. Bos, Léo Ducas, Eike Kiltz, Tancrède Lepoint, Vadim Lyubashevsky, John M. Schanck, Peter Schwabe, Gregor Seiler, Damien Stehlé

sources.ref_file_title: HHK17 - A Modular Analysis of the Fujisaki-Okamoto Transformation
sources.authors: Dennis Hofheinz, Kathrin Hövelmanns, Eike Kiltz
sources.note: cryptobib_key: TCC:HofHovKil17 (verified in vendor/cryptobib/crypto.bib, pp. 341-371). Companion rather than follow-up: the modular FO analysis (ROM and QROM) that Kyber's IND-CCA proof invokes.

pages.class_justification: No source states an RTV-style class; the IND-CCA proof goes through the Fujisaki–Okamoto transform in an idealized (random-oracle) model, which the RTV taxonomy does not classify.
pages.model_justification: The IND-CPA scheme is standard-model from Module LWE, but the IND-CCA KEM claim — the conclusion of this edge — is proved via a Fujisaki–Okamoto transform with implicit rejection in the random-oracle model (QROM bounds also given). Frontmatter currently says standard and must change to rom.
pages.statement: Kyber, the basis of ML-KEM (FIPS 203), is an [[key-encapsulation-mechanism#ind-cca-security|IND-CCA-secure]] [[key-encapsulation-mechanism|KEM]] in the random-oracle model assuming hardness of [[learning-with-errors#module-lwe|Module LWE]] (module rank $k \in \{2,3,4\}$ in the proposed parameter sets): an IND-CPA public-key encryption scheme from Module LWE is converted into an IND-CCA KEM by a Fujisaki–Okamoto transform with implicit rejection; the ROM reduction is tight, the QROM reduction is not — [[BDK+18 - CRYSTALS-Kyber A CCA-Secure Module-Lattice-Based KEM|BDK+18]].
pages.sketch: The CPA scheme is LPR-style over a module: the public key is $(\mathbf{A}, \mathbf{t} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{s} + \mathbf{e})$ and a ciphertext is a pair of compressed Module LWE samples carrying the message in the high-order bits, so key and ciphertext are pseudorandom under Module LWE. The FO transform derives the encryption randomness and the session key by hashing the message; decapsulation re-encrypts and, on mismatch, outputs a pseudorandom key derived from a secret seed (implicit rejection), giving IND-CCA in the ROM.
pages.improvements_text: - Kyber's IND-CCA proof instantiates the modular Fujisaki–Okamoto analysis, which supplies the ROM and QROM bounds — [[HHK17 - A Modular Analysis of the Fujisaki-Okamoto Transformation|HHK17]].

sources.ref_file_title: LS15 - Worst-case to average-case reductions for module lattices
sources.note: Defines Module LWE and notes that rank 1 specializes to Ring LWE (and ring degree 1 to plain LWE).

pages.class_justification: Both directions are the identity: a rank-1 Module LWE instance is a Ring LWE instance and vice versa, so instances and adversaries pass through unchanged — one fixed construction and one fixed reduction, each using its input only as an oracle.
pages.statement: [[learning-with-errors#module-lwe|Module LWE]] at module rank $k = 1$ is [[learning-with-errors#ring-lwe|Ring LWE]]: a rank-1 module over $R_q$ is $R_q$ itself, so the two sample distributions coincide and the problems are identical — [[LS15 - Worst-case to average-case reductions for module lattices|LS15]].
pages.sketch: A rank-1 Module LWE sample $(\mathbf{a}, \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{s} \rangle + e)$ with $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{s} \in R_q$ is a Ring LWE sample $(a, a \cdot s + e)$; the identity map is a reduction in both directions.
flags: Definitional coincidence presumes matching conventions: LS15's M-LWE at rank 1 is LPR10's R-LWE (same dual-ring and error-distribution setup); the wiki's Module LWE and Ring LWE sections use the same non-dual convention, so they coincide as written.
Hypothesis node module-lwe-rank-1 resolves via the learning-with-errors frontmatter variant alias to #module-lwe; a dedicated anchor would make the rank-1 qualifier addressable.

The migrated LS15 editorial quote also contains the incorrect 'k = n recovers plain LWE' claim, handled as wrong_claim on module-lwe-to-lwe-ls15; only the k = 1 half is correct and it is the content of this page.
No page for the converse direction exists in content/Reductions/, so kind: equivalence is appropriate.
verifier_changes: statement, sketch and source note tightened; flag added confirming no converse page exists

pages.wrong_reason: 'Module LWE at rank k = n recovers plain LWE' (over a degree-n polynomial ring $R_q$) is false as stated: a rank-n module over a degree-n ring has $\ZZ_q$-dimension $n^2$, and the sample matrix is block-structured (negacyclic blocks), not uniform, so rank-n Module LWE is neither syntactically nor known to be computationally equivalent to plain LWE in dimension $n$ (or $n^2$). Plain LWE is the specialization of Module LWE at ring degree 1 ($R = \ZZ$) with arbitrary module rank — the definitional edge LS15 actually supports (rank 1 recovers ring problems, degree 1 recovers unstructured problems). The source page learning-with-errors.md line 135 carries the same error: its parenthetical '$R_q \cong \ZZ_q^n$' is a module isomorphism, not a ring isomorphism, and does not remove the multiplicative structure.
flags: Correct replacement edge: Module LWE over R = Z (ring degree 1) at rank n <=> LWE, definitional, source LS15; the hypothesis node would need redefining (module-lwe-rank-n currently aliases to #module-lwe with the wrong reading).

learning-with-errors.md § Module LWE bullet 'When k = n: recovers plain LWE (fully unstructured, ring R_q ≅ Z_q^n)' needs the same fix (skeptical-checker lane); shortest-integer-solution.md § Module-SIS makes the analogous 'k = n recovers plain SIS' claim.

Nontrivial relations between Module LWE and Ring LWE/LWE exist — e.g. Albrecht–Deo, 'Large Modulus Ring-LWE ≥ Module-LWE' (ASIACRYPT 2017) — but they are different edges with different parameters, not this equivalence.
